notes.text: Tabitha, which is by interpretation Dorcas — She was probably a Hellenist Jew, known among the Hebrews by the Syriac name Tabitha, while the Greeks called her in their own language, Dorcas. They are both words of the same import, and signify a roe or fawn.
The disciples sent to him — Probably none of those at Joppa had the gift of miracles. Nor is it certain that they expected a miracle from him.
While she was with the in — That is, before she died.

Peter having put them all out — That he might have the better opportunity of wrestling with God in prayer, said, Tabitha, arise. And she opened her eyes, and seeing Peter, sat up - Who can imagine the surprise of Dorcas, when called back to life? Or of her friends, when they saw her alive? For the sake of themselves, and of the poor, there was cause of rejoicing, and much more, for such a confirmation of the Gospel. Yet to herself it was matter of resignation, not joy, to be called back to these scenes of vanity: but doubtless, her remaining days were still more zealously spent in the service of her saviour and her God. Thus was a richer treasure laid up for her in heaven, and she afterward returned to a more exceeding weight of glory, than that from which so astonishing a providence had recalled her for a season.

glossa.text:
*Named Tabitha. ((RAB.))* Tabitha is rendered from the Hebrew into Latin *Dorcas,* or *Damula,* as is found in *quisbusdam* copies.

*Dorcas.* Allegorically: Dorcas is a doe or a roe: and it signifies the soul, lofty by the pursuit of virtue, but contemptible in the opinion of men. But Luke, in setting down the interpretation of the name, signifies that a mystery is contained in it. These animals, dwelling in the mountains, see sharply: whence from the sharpness of their sight they are called dorcades in Greek. So they who are lofty by the merits of their works aim at higher things, and watch circumspectly over themselves, they live simply with a discerning degree of work, they walk as it were with a cloven hoof, they ruminate the word of God by assiduous meditation.
*In an upper room. ((RAB.))* She is placed in a higher place, either because of the height of her merit, or because of the sublimity of the miracle which was to be wrought upon her.

*All being put forth. ((ID.))* This was done after the example of Christ raising up the daughter of the chief ruler of the synagogue, to avoid elation, or lest the unworthy should see the sign. *She opened. ((BEDA.))* Right is the order of those that rise again, that first she open the eyes of the mind, afterwards, the voice of Peter being known, she sit up, and receive again the lost light of her circumspection, that she may live unto the teaching of those who help. *She opened her eyes.* These are the three degrees of the raising up.
*And giving.* Tabitha rises again at the touch of Peter's hand, because the soul lying sick in sins grows strong again by no better way than by the examples of the saints.

notes.text: Lie down — To repose myself at noon, as the manner was in those hot countries. Green - Where there is both delight and plenty of provisions.
Restoreth — Hebrew. He bringeth it back; from its errors and wandering. For - Not for any worth in me, but for the glory of his justice, and faithfulness, and goodness.
Thy rod and thy staff — Two words denoting the same thing, and both designing God's pastoral care over him.

A table — Thou furnishest me with plenty of provisions and comforts. Oil - With aromatic ointments, which were then used at great feasts; thy comforts delight my soul. Runneth over - Thou hast given me a plentiful portions, signified by the cup, given to the guests by the master of the feast. This psalm is generally thought to have been composed by David, upon bringing the ark of God from the house of Obed- edom, into the tabernacle which David had built for it, 2 Sam. vi, 12, 17. Wherein he hath a farther prospect to the temple, which he earnestly desired and intended to build. Moreover because the tabernacle, and temple, and ark, were types of Christ, and of his church and of heaven. David extended his thoughts to them also, or at least the Holy Ghost designed to comprehend them under these typical expressions. He shews God's sovereignty over the world, ver. 1, 2. Who shall receive his blessing, ver. 3-6. An exhortation to receive Christ, ver. 7-10. A psalm of David.

glossa.text: *A psalm of David.* ((CASS.)) The Prophet foretold the return of the people from Babylon. *The Lord ruleth me.* A psalm of mercy, enumerating ten graces, that all may hope in the mercy of God. ((AUG.)) The Church speaks of Christ.

*In a place of pasture.* ((CASS.)) The first grace, a place of pasture, that is, the divine word, which fattens those who meditate upon it. *Upon the water.* The second grace, the water of refreshment.

*My soul.* ((ID.)) The third grace, etc., *as far as* but first he brought me up upon the water of refreshment, first he converted my soul. *He hath led.* ((ID.)) The fourth, in that he led me upon the precepts of charity. *Upon the paths.* ((AUG.)) The narrower commandments and the more perfect counsels; as it were upon paths few just men walk, even as paths are narrower than roads.

*For though I shall walk.* ((CASS.)) The fifth, that in the shadow of death he fears no evils. *Thou art with me.* ((AUG.)) In the heart by faith, that after the shadow of death I may be with thee. *Thy rod.* ((CASS.)) The sixth, correction; or the rod is strictness, which converts vices. The staff is governance, which upholds the faithful.

*Thou hast prepared in my sight.* ((CASS.)) The seventh, the table of the Lord, the blessed banqueting, the fullness of faith, the heavenly food, of which the Apostle: *He that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh judgment to himself. In my sight a table:* even if not that of the wicked. Of this it is said: *But these at the table of the rich man,* that is, of Christ, *know that thou too must prepare the like,* that is, to suffer as he did. *Thou hast anointed:* the eighth, the anointing of the head, namely of Christ, which was dried up by no barrenness of sin, whence the rest of the members rejoice, because from the head the ointment ran down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, and unto the skirt of his garment. *And my chalice.* The ninth, the chalice, the blood of Christ, which so inebriates that it makes men sober. *Mine,* because I receive it. Or, thine, because thou givest it. The table and the chalice, flesh and blood, although they are one sacrament, yet under diverse species, because both are taken, are here set down separately.
*And mercy.* ((CASS.)) The tenth, mercy following after unto keeping, which goes before unto the conferring of grace.
*And that I may dwell.* ((HIER.)) This is joined to all the things above. As though: thou hast placed, thou hast brought up, thou hast led, etc., and this to the end that I may dwell.

notes.text: A great multitude — Of those who had happily finished their course. Such multitudes are afterwards described, and still higher degrees of glory which they attain after a sharp fight and magnificent victory, chap. xiv, 1; xv, 2; xix, 1; xx, 4. There is an inconceivable variety in the degrees of reward in the other world. Let not any slothful one say, "If I get to heaven at all, I will be content:" such an one may let heaven go altogether. In worldly things, men are ambitious to get as high as they can. Christians have a far more noble ambition. The difference between the very highest and the lowest state in the world is nothing to the smallest difference between the degrees of glory. But who has time to think of this? Who is at all concerned about it? Standing before the throne - In the full vision of God. And palms in their hands - Tokens of joy and victory.

Salvation to our God — Who hath saved us from all evil into all the happiness of heaven. The salvation for which they praise God is described, verse 15; that for which they praise the Lamb, verse 14; and both, in the sixteenth and seventeenth verses. ver. 16, 17

And all the angels stood — In waiting. Round about the throne, and the elders and the four living creatures - That is, the living creatures, next the throne; the elders, round these; and the angels, round them both. And they fell on their faces - So do the elders, once only, chap. xi, 16. The heavenly ceremonial has its fixed order and measure.

Amen — With this word all the angels confirm the words of the "great multitude;" but they likewise carry the praise much higher. The blessing, and the glory, and the wisdom, and the thanksgiving, and the honour, and the power, and the strength, be unto our God forever and ever - Before the Lamb began to open the seven seals, a sevenfold hymn of praise was brought him by many angels, chap. v, 12. Now he is upon opening the last seal, and the seven angels are going to receive seven trumpets, in order to make the kingdoms of the world subject to God. All the angels give sevenfold praise to God.

And one of the elders — What stands, verses 13-17, ver. 13-17 might have immediately followed the tenth verse; but that the praise of the angels, which was at the same time with that of the "great multitude," came in between. Answered - He answered St. John's desire to know, not any words that he spoke.

My Lord — Or, my master; a common term of respect. So Zechariah, likewise, bespeaks the angel, Zech. i, 9; iv, 4; vi, 4. Thou knowest - That is, I know not; but thou dost. These are they - Not martyrs; for these are not such a multitude as no man can number. But as all the angels appear here, so do all the souls of the righteous who had lived from the beginning of the world. Who come - He does not say, who did come; but, who come now also: to whom, likewise, pertain all who will come hereafter. Out of great affliction - Of various kinds, wisely and graciously allotted by God to all his children. And have washed their robes - From all guilt. And made them white - In all holiness. By the blood of the Lamb - Which not only cleanses, but adorns us also.

Therefore — Because they came out of great affliction, and have washed their robes in his blood. Are they before the throne - It seems, even nearer than the angels. And serve him day and night - Speaking after the manner of men; that is, continually. In his temple - Which is in heaven. And he shall have his tent over them - Shall spread his glory over them as a covering.
Neither shall the sun light on them — For God is there their sun. Nor any painful heat, or inclemency of seasons.

For the Lamb will feed them — With eternal peace and joy; so that they shall hunger no more. And will lead them to living fountains of water - The comforts of the Holy Ghost; so that they shall thirst no more. Neither shall they suffer or grieve any more; for God "will wipe away all tears from their eyes."

glossa.text: *After these things.* When he had seen, according to the figure, those to be marked out under a certain number, and only from the children of Israel, now he openly teaches that by that number all the faithful, and by the twelve tribes all the nations, are to be understood. *Standing.* Namely, ready to obey God the judge, or their prelates also. This in the present.
*Salvation to our God who sitteth.* Not through ourselves, but through the Lamb do we have salvation, that is, the remission of sins, and good working, and eternal glory.

*And all.* By the angels spoken of above, the greater prelates can be understood; by these, the lesser prelates, or subjects only, as there are angels and archangels, and yet all are angels, that is, messengers. But even now there are greater and lesser prelates, that is, archbishops and bishops.

*Amen.* As if he should say: If you attribute it to God, you do well. Or *amen* will be read with what follows: *Amen,* that is, truth in the things premised, and *benediction,* that is, the exaltation which he has above every creature, or our exaltation in the virtues: and *brightness,* that is, impassibility, or yours in works.
*And one answered.* The multitude having been seen in so great dignity, he is moved to consider by what way it was able to ascend thither, that he may teach others to look upon the same.
*Their robes,* etc. The innocence received in baptism, or their bodies.
*They shall not hunger, nor thirst,* etc. He who gave knowledge to the angels will give the same knowledge to them also.

*He shall lead them to the fountains of the waters of life,* etc. And by this he shall lead them in time to come to refreshment of every kind. *God shall wipe away every tear.* Every grief, whether for their own offences, or for adversities, or exile, or other things of this sort.

notes.text: It was the feast of the dedication — Instituted by Judas Maccabeus, 1 Macc. iv, 59, when he purged and dedicated the altar and temple after they had been polluted. So our Lord observed festivals even of human appointment. Is it not, at least, innocent for us to do the same?

In Solomon's portico — Josephus informs us, that when Solomon built the temple, he filled up a part of the adjacent valley, and built a portico over it toward the east. This was a noble structure, supported by a wall four hundred cubits high: and continued even to the time of Albinus and Agrippa, which was several years after the death of Christ.

Ye do not believe, because ye are not of my sheep — Because ye do not, will not follow me: because ye are proud, unholy, lovers of praise, lovers of the world, lovers of pleasure, not of God. 27, 28, 29. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me, &c.- Our Lord still alludes to the discourse he had before this festival. As if he had said, My sheep are they who,

1. Hear my voice by faith;

2. Are known (that is, approved) by me, as loving me; and

3. Follow me, keep my commandments, with a believing, loving heart. And to those who,

1. Truly believe (observe three promises annexed to three conditions) I give eternal life. He does not say, I will, but I give. For he that believeth hath everlasting life. Those whom,

2. I know truly to love me, shall never perish, provided they abide in my love.

3. Those who follow me, neither men nor devils can pluck out of my hand. My Father who hath, by an unchangeable decree, given me all that believe, love, and obey, is greater than all in heaven or earth, and none is able to pluck them out of his hand.

I and the Father are one — Not by consent of will only, but by unity of power, and consequently of nature. Are - This word confutes Sabellius, proving the plurality of persons: one - This word confutes Arius, proving the unity of nature in God. Never did any prophet before, from the beginning of the world, use any one expression of himself, which could possibly be so interpreted as this and other expressions were, by all that heard our Lord speak. Therefore if he was not God he must have been the vilest of men.

glossa.text: *And it was the feast of the dedication,* etc. Caenon, that is, new. Hence encaenia, that is, to inaugurate. The encaenia is the feast of the dedication of the temple, which was made by Judas Maccabaeus in the time of winter. And winter is mentioned here that it may signify the Jews as cold, who do not come to the fire, that is, do not believe in Christ. Solomon, when the temple was built, dedicated it in autumn ((III Reg. VIII)). Zorobabel and Jesus the priest dedicated the rebuilt temple after the captivity, in spring ((II Esdr. VI)). Judas Maccabaeus, for the profanation of Antiochus, in winter ((I Machab. IV)).
*In the porch.* The porches with which the temple was girded are wont to be signified by the name of the temple.

*The Jews therefore came round about him.* While the Lord patiently preached the truth amid reproaches, the blinded do not obey but tempt him: *How long dost thou take away our soul?* They falsely charge with taking away souls him who saves them; whom they thought a mere man, but one who would reign before all. *If thou be the Christ, tell us plainly.* They do not desire the truth, but prepare a calumny, that if he should say he was a king, they might deliver him to the power as one acting against Augustus. But the Lord so tempers his answer that there is no place of calumny for them, and that to the faithful, for whose sake these things are recounted, it may appear plainly that he himself is the Christ, not a man only, as they think, but the Son of God.
*And no man can snatch them out of my Father's hand.* Because from this, that I am of the Father, I am greater for protecting than they for assailing.
*I and the Father are one.* By these words he not only resolves the question of the Jews, who came in order to tempt him, but also condemns the madness of the heretics to come.

sermons.title: Upon Our Lords Sermon on the Mount II
sermons.author: John Wesley

hymns.title: The Lord's my shepherd, I'll not want
The King of love my shepherd is
Deck thyself, my soul, with gladness

echoes.text: When Elisha had come into the house, behold, the child was dead, and laid on his bed. He went in therefore, and shut the door on them both, and prayed to Yahweh. He went up, and lay on the child, and put his mouth on his mouth, and his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. He stretched himself on him; and the flesh of the child grew warm. Then he returned, and walked in the house once back and forth; and went up, and stretched himself on him. Then […]
echoes.note: Elisha enters the room where the dead child lies, puts everyone out, prays, and the child opens her/his eyes. 'Peter sent them all out, and knelt down and prayed... he said, Tabitha, get up! She opened her eyes' matches the sequence point-for-point: privacy, prayer, command, the opening of the eyes. Highest-volume parallel in the pericope.

echoes.text: After these things, the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, fell sick; and his sickness was so severe, that there was no breath left in him. She said to Elijah, “What have I to do with you, you man of God? You have come to me to bring my sin to memory, and to kill my son!” He said to her, “Give me your son.” He took him out of her bosom, and carried him up into the room where he stayed, and laid him on his own bed. He cried to Yahweh, and said, […]
echoes.note: Elijah raises the widow's son, who is laid in the upper room (loft) where the prophet prays; the result is faith ('now I know'). Tabitha is laid in an upper room, surrounded by widows, raised through Peter's prayer, and 'many believed.' Strong coherence: upper room + widow context + prayer + resurrection + resulting belief.

echoes.text: It fell on a day, that Elisha passed to Shunem, where there was a prominent woman; and she persuaded him to eat bread. So it was, that as often as he passed by, he turned in there to eat bread. She said to her husband, “See now, I perceive that this is a holy man of God, that passes by us continually. Please let us make a little room on the wall. Let us set for him there a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp stand. It shall be, when he comes to us, that he […]
echoes.note: Beyond the resuscitation itself, the Shunammite cycle frames the dead one laid in a prepared upper chamber and messengers sent urgently to fetch the man of God ('do not slacken your riding'); Joppa's disciples 'sent two men... imploring him not to delay.' The send-for-the-prophet-without-delay motif reinforces the Elisha typology.

spans.label: Tarsus & Antioch
spans.note: Sent home to Tarsus, then fetched by Barnabas to teach at Antioch, where the disciples were first called Christians. Ends with the famine-relief visit to Jerusalem.

places.name: Lydda
places.id: Modern Lod on the eastern Sharon plain, an Iron Age and post-exilic Jewish town (Neh 11:35 Lod). Renamed Diospolis under Hadrian. Continuous habitation; the modern Israeli town preserves the name.

places.name: Joppa
places.id: Tel Yafo (Jaffa) on the Mediterranean coast, the natural harbor for Jerusalem. Listed in Thutmose III's Karnak topographical list and in the Amarna letters.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Yahweh brought him outside, and said, “Look now toward the sky, and count the stars, if you are able to count them.” He said to Abram, “So will your seed be.”
echoes.note: The Abrahamic promise: "count the stars, if you are able to count them... so shall your offspring be" — the uncountable, innumerable seed. John's "a great multitude, which no man could count" (hon arithmesai auton oudeis edynato) directly fulfills the count-if-you-can promise, now extended beyond Israel to every nation. Strong on volume and on John's larger Abrahamic-fulfillment logic (the multitude completes what the sealed 144,000 represent).

echoes.text: I will make your offspring as the dust of the earth, so that if a man can number the dust of the earth, then your seed may also be numbered.
echoes.note: Parallel Abrahamic promise: offspring "as the dust of the earth, which if a man can number..." — the explicit "if a man can number" idiom that John negates ("which no man could count"). LXX ei dynatai tis exarithmesai is verbally close to John's clause. Pairs with Gen 15:5 as the twin innumerability promises being eschatologically realized.

echoes.text: You shall take on the first day the fruit of goodly trees, branches of palm trees, and boughs of thick trees, and willows of the brook; and you shall rejoice before Yahweh your God seven days.
echoes.note: The palm branches (phoinikes) in the multitude's hands evoke the Feast of Tabernacles/Sukkot, where worshipers take "branches of palm trees" and rejoice before the LORD — fitting the booth/tabernacle imagery that immediately follows (7:15, God spreading his tabernacle, skenosei). Festal-joy and ingathering-harvest coherence is strong; the specific lulav connection is the principal reason this is an allusion not a mere echo.

echoes.text: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: "all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him" (Aram./Theod. laoi, phylai, glossai) — Daniel's stereotyped fourfold list of the nations is the template for John's recurrent "every nation, tribe, people, and language" formula (cf. Rev 5:9; 13:7). The multitude drawn from all peoples fulfills Daniel's universal dominion of the Son of Man. Recurrence in Revelation strengthens the link.

echoes.text: And he entered into it on the three and twentieth day of the second month, in the hundred and seventy and first year, with praise and palm branches, and with harps, and with cymbals, and with viols, and with hymns, and with songs: because a great enemy was destroyed out of Israel.
echoes.note: Simon's triumphal entry into the Jerusalem citadel "with praise and palm branches (baia)... and with hymns and songs" — Second-Temple precedent for palm branches as the gesture of victory celebration and deliverance, illuminating why the redeemed multitude (victors out of tribulation) bear palms while acclaiming salvation. Confirms the victory-procession nuance alongside the Tabernacles nuance (cf. also 2 Macc 10:7; John 12:13).

echoes.text: Salvation belongs to Yahweh. Your blessing be on your people. Selah.
echoes.note: "Salvation belongs to the LORD" (LXX Ps 3:9, tou kyriou he soteria) — the acclamation "Salvation be to our God" closely mirrors this psalmic confession that deliverance is God's alone. Idiom is common across the Psalter (cf. Ps 37:39; Jonah 2:9), so attribution to a single verse is uncertain, but the verbal shape is closest here.

echoes.text: Yours, Yahweh, is the greatness, the power, the glory, the victory, and the majesty! For all that is in the heavens and in the earth is yours. Yours is the kingdom, Yahweh, and you are exalted as head above all.
echoes.note: David's doxology — "Yours, O LORD, is the greatness and the power and the glory... and the majesty... blessing" — a sevenfold-style ascription of attributes to God that stands behind the seven-membered doxology of 7:12 (blessing, glory, wisdom, thanksgiving, honor, power, might). Liturgical-doxological coherence; faint as a specific citation since such ascriptions are formulaic.

echoes.text: In the year that king Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up; and his train filled the temple. Above him stood the seraphim. Each one had six wings. With two he covered his face. With two he covered his feet. With two he flew. One called to another, and said, “Holy, holy, holy, is Yahweh of Armies! The whole earth is full of his glory!”
echoes.note: The throne-vision with surrounding heavenly beings prostrate/crying praise underlies the angels, elders, and four living creatures falling before the throne; the living creatures themselves derive from Isa 6 seraphim and Ezek 1/10. Faint here because the throne-room cast is established earlier (Rev 4) rather than newly drawn from Isaiah in this verse.

echoes.text: They shall not hunger nor thirst; neither shall the heat nor sun strike them: for he who has mercy on them will lead them, even by springs of water he will guide them.
echoes.note: "They shall not hunger nor thirst, neither scorching heat nor sun shall strike them, for he who has pity on them will lead them, and by springs of water will guide them" — the densest verbal source in the chapter. John reproduces all four elements in order: no hunger, no thirst, no sun/scorching heat smiting them, and a shepherd-guide leading to springs of water. Hays' criteria max out (volume, recurrence of the Servant-shepherd motif, coherence with the new-exodus ingathering). LXX peinasousin... dipsesousin... kausön... pegas hydaton tracks John closely.

echoes.text: He has swallowed up death forever! The Lord Yahweh will wipe away tears from off all faces. He will take the reproach of his people away from off all the earth, for Yahweh has spoken it.
echoes.note: "He will swallow up death forever, and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces" — direct source for "God will wipe away every tear from their eyes" (exaleipsei... pan dakryon). The eschatological consolation at the victory-banquet on the mountain. High verbal volume; recurs at Rev 21:4. Note the MT "swallow up death" vs. LXX katepien ho thanatos ischysas; John follows the tear-wiping clause closely regardless of the textual divergence in the first colon.

echoes.text: I will set up one shepherd over them, and he shall feed them, even my servant David; he shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd.
echoes.note: "I will set up over them one shepherd... my servant David, and he shall feed them and be their shepherd" — the messianic Davidic-shepherd promise underlying "the Lamb... shepherds them." Striking oxymoron (the Lamb is the Shepherd) fuses Ezekiel 34's shepherd-king with John's Lamb-Christology. Strong coherence; Ezek 34:23 cited as the principal verse of the chapter-long shepherd oracle.

echoes.text: Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters.
echoes.note: "The LORD is my shepherd... he leads me beside still waters" (LXX Ps 22:1-2, hodegesen me epi hydatos anapauseos) — the shepherd-leads-to-water image directly behind "shepherds them, and leads (hodegesei) them to springs of life-giving waters." John's hodegeo echoes the psalm's verb. High volume and coherence with the Isa 49 / Ezek 34 shepherd cluster.

echoes.text: Binding his foal to the vine, his donkey’s colt to the choice vine; he has washed his garments in wine, his robes in the blood of grapes.
echoes.note: Judah's blessing: "he washed his garments in wine and his robe in the blood of grapes" — the only OT image of washing a robe in (grape-)blood, giving John the paradoxical "washed their robes... white in the Lamb's blood." Coheres with the Judah/Lion-Lamb Christology and ties pericope 7.4 back to the Judah-first tribal list (7.2). The blood-of-grapes/blood-of-the-Lamb figural link is medium-to-strong on coherence though contested on verbal volume.

echoes.text: “Come now, and let us reason together,” says Yahweh: “Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow. Though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.
echoes.note: "Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow" — the prophetic image of sin-cleansing producing whiteness underlies robes "made white" through the Lamb's blood (cleansing-unto-whiteness). Coheres with the purification motif; medium volume since John supplies the paradoxical agent (blood) absent from Isaiah.

echoes.text: Many shall purify themselves, and make themselves white, and be refined; but the wicked shall do wickedly; and none of the wicked shall understand; but those who are wise shall understand.
echoes.note: "Many shall purify themselves and make themselves white (LXX leukanthosin) and be refined" through the time of trouble — the closest source for the eschatological making-white of the faithful precisely amid tribulation, matching "made them white" of those who "came out of the great tribulation." Daniel's end-time-refining-whitening is thematically and verbally apt (leukaino).

echoes.text: Some of those who are wise shall fall, to refine them, and to purify, and to make them white, even to the time of the end; because it is yet for the time appointed.
echoes.note: "Some of the wise shall stumble, to refine and purify them and to make them white (LXX leukanai), until the time of the end" — companion to Dan 12:10; the wise are whitened/refined through persecution. Reinforces the tribulation-purification reading of the white-robed multitude. Cited alongside 12:10 as the Danielic whitening pair.

echoes.text: “At that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people; and there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time: and at that time your people shall be delivered, everyone who shall be found written in the book.
echoes.note: "there shall be a time of trouble (LXX thlipsis / Theod. hemera thlipseos) such as never has been" — the eschatological great distress that John names "the great tribulation" (tes thlipseos tes megales). Daniel supplies the technical term and the deliver-the-named-remnant frame; coherent with the sealing/deliverance arc of the whole chapter.

echoes.text: I will set my tent among you, and my soul won’t abhor you. I will walk among you, and will be your God, and you will be my people.
echoes.note: "I will make my dwelling (LXX skenen) among you... and I will walk among you" — the covenant-presence/tabernacling promise behind "He who sits on the throne will spread his tabernacle (skenosei) over them." Part of the dwelling-of-God-with-his-people stream (Ezek 37:27; cf. Rev 21:3). Medium coherence; the skene cognate strengthens it.

echoes.text: My tent also shall be with them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
echoes.note: "My dwelling place (LXX kataskenosis) shall be with them, and I will be their God" — the eschatological tabernacling-with-the-redeemed promise, near-synonymous with Lev 26:11 and directly echoed in the skenoo of 7:15 (and again Rev 21:3). Reinforces the new-covenant-presence reading.

echoes.text: Yahweh will create over the whole habitation of Mount Zion, and over her assemblies, a cloud and smoke by day, and the shining of a flaming fire by night; for over all the glory will be a canopy. There will be a pavilion for a shade in the daytime from the heat, and for a refuge and for a shelter from storm and from rain.
echoes.note: Over Zion a canopy/booth (LXX skepe) for "shade from the heat" and shelter — combines the tabernacle-spread-over-them and the no-scorching-heat motifs in a single Zion-protection oracle, paralleling 7:15-16. Faint but apposite; possibly part of the cluster behind John's protective-canopy imagery.

echoes.text: Yahweh is your keeper. Yahweh is your shade on your right hand. The sun will not harm you by day, nor the moon by night.
echoes.note: "The LORD is your keeper... the sun shall not strike you by day, nor the moon by night" — the sun-shall-not-strike-you protection paralleling "neither will the sun beat on them." Idiomatically close but likely mediated through Isa 49:10, which John follows more fully; cited as a secondary witness.

echoes.text: Seven women shall take hold of one man in that day, saying, “We will eat our own bread, and wear our own clothing: only let us be called by your name. Take away our reproach.”
echoes.note: Faint: white-garment/clean-robe symbolism of the purified Zion-remnant in Isa 4 (the branch made glorious, the survivors called holy) coheres with the white-robed survivors of tribulation; included as a contested ingathering-of-the-holy-remnant resonance rather than a verbal source.

echoes.text: “For my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the spring of living waters, and cut them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.
echoes.note: "the fountain of living waters" (LXX pegen hydatos zoes) — Jeremiah's image of God as the living-water source colors "springs of life-giving waters" (pegas hydaton zoes); the phrase also runs through Ps 36:9, Zech 14:8, and John 4/7. Common idiom, so single-verse attribution is uncertain; cited as the closest verbal match.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: But Judas and his kindred said, Behold, our enemies are discomfited: let us go up to cleanse the holy place, and to dedicate it afresh. And all the army was gathered together, and they went up to mount Sion. And they saw the sanctuary laid desolate, and the altar profaned, and the gates burned up, and shrubs growing in the courts as in a forest or as on one of the mountains, and the priests’ chambers pulled down; and they tore their clothes, and made […]
echoes.note: The Feast of the Dedication (Hanukkah) commemorates Judas Maccabeus' cleansing and rededication of the temple altar, the festival's institution. John's explicit setting at this feast (v.22) frames Jesus, the one whom the Father 'consecrated' (v.36), as the true dedicated/sanctified one. High availability as Second-Temple background.

echoes.text: And Maccabaeus and those who were with him, the Lord leading them on, recovered the temple and the city; and they pulled down the altars that had been built in the marketplace by the aliens, and also the walls of sacred inclosures. And having cleansed the sanctuary they made another altar of sacrifice; and striking stones and taking fire out of them, they offered sacrifices, after they had ceased for two years, and burned incense, and lighted lamps, and […]
echoes.note: Parallel account of the purification and rededication of the temple and the eight-day festival 'in the manner of Tabernacles,' establishing the Dedication setting. Reinforces 1 Macc 4 as the festival's narrative grounding for John's winter feast.

echoes.text: For thus says the Lord Yahweh: Behold, I myself, even I, will search for my sheep, and will seek them out. As a shepherd seeks out his flock in the day that he is among his sheep that are scattered abroad, so will I seek out my sheep; and I will deliver them out of all places where they have been scattered in the cloudy and dark day. I will bring them out from the peoples, and gather them from the countries, and will bring them into their own land; and I […]
echoes.note: 'My sheep hear my voice... and they follow me' (v.27) restates the LORD's own knowing and gathering of his flock from Ezekiel 34, now claimed by Jesus. The sustained shepherd theme links the Dedication confrontation back to the discourse's governing subtext.

echoes.text: Yes, since the day was I am he; and there is no one who can deliver out of my hand. I will work, and who can hinder it?”
echoes.note: 'There is no one who can deliver out of my hand' undergirds 'no one will snatch them out of my hand' (v.28) and 'out of my Father's hand' (v.29). The security-in-the-divine-hand idiom is a deliberate divine self-claim applied to Jesus.

echoes.text: “See now that I myself am he. There is no god with me. I kill and I make alive. I wound and I heal. There is no one who can deliver out of my hand.
echoes.note: 'There is no one who can deliver out of my hand' (the same idiom) with 'I kill and I make alive' stands behind Jesus giving eternal life and holding the sheep inviolably. Reinforces the divine-hand security motif alongside Isaiah.

echoes.text: Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one.
echoes.note: 'Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one' resonates behind 'I and the Father are one' (v.30). The Shema's oneness language is reframed christologically; coherent with the blasphemy charge that follows, though the unity claimed is functional/relational.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Christ is risen!
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want.
He leads us beside still waters.
My sheep hear my voice, and they follow me;
and no one can snatch them out of his hand.
Come to the green pastures, come to the table he spreads.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Come and lie down in the green grass where the shepherd has led you, the noise of the week left behind.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
Listen — under all the other voices there is one you know, calling you each by name.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
He leads you beside still water and sets a table in the open, and your cup runs over.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
And the Lamb at the center of the throne becomes your shepherd, guiding you to springs of living water, wiping every tear away.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
So follow the voice that goodness and mercy follow, all the way home:
Christ is risen, Alleluia!

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
His voice calls us by name, and we know it.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
He leads us beside still waters, his table spread.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
Goodness and mercy follow us; come, let us worship.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
